messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Martin Weiss is a 68-year-old psychologist who has been married for decades, and it is still difficult for him to speak plainly about the relationship in which he was assaulted by a romantic partner. What he can describe comes in fragments. He remembers the bicycle first: it had been knocked sideways in the hallway outside the apartment after an argument, the front wheel still slowly turning while she stood over him in clothes he now cannot bring himself to wear anything resembling. He can call up sharp visual stills—the angle of the wheel, the fabric at her wrist, the cramped entryway—but not a continuous account of how one moment became the next. At other times there is no image at all, only a sudden wash of the same dread and humiliation. Those broken, photographic pieces have left him feeling that his old assumptions about intimacy, safety, and even his own judgment were destroyed; if he could be trapped and hurt in what he thought was a loving relationship, then people are not what they seem, and something in him must be fundamentally inadequate for having missed it.

In the months after he left that relationship, the world began to organize itself around reminders. Passing a bicycle chained outside his office building could stop him short. Riding public transportation, especially when pressed in among strangers, brought back the trapped feeling of that apartment hallway. What unsettled him most, and what he is ashamed to admit, is being alone with women in enclosed spaces. In his work as a psychologist, this has become painfully concrete: he notices his body tense when a female patient is the last appointment of the day and the waiting room has emptied out. In those moments the trigger does not remain a simple reminder. It lands immediately on the conclusions he has already drawn—people can turn dangerous without warning, he cannot trust his own reading of them, he may not be able to protect himself—and the reminder feels like proof that the world is still unsafe.

Because he has come to believe both that others are deceptive and that he himself is not equal to managing what happened, Martin works hard to keep tight control over his internal life. He never allows himself to feel or express anger, especially toward women, as if letting himself register it would make him lose control or reveal something ugly about him. He monitors his face and voice in sessions, keeps his feelings flattened, and avoids wearing clothes that resemble what he had on during the assault. When a bicycle appears unexpectedly on the street, or he finds himself hemmed in by a crowd, he becomes even more deliberate about containing himself, gripping hard to composure and pushing down whatever rises in him.

That effort has not made him feel safer. If anything, Martin has become preoccupied with danger. He watches other people closely for signs that they might harm him, scanning changes in expression, stance, tone, and proximity. Crowded places are especially difficult because there are too many people to track; being alone with a woman can feel intolerably exposing because all of his attention narrows onto whether he is missing some threat. Nights are worse. He wakes and checks whether he is safe, listening to the house, looking toward the bedroom door, more alert after dark than during the day. The more he lives in this state of vigilance, the more convinced he becomes that his earlier beliefs were naive, that danger hides in ordinary encounters, and that his sensitivity is necessary because he cannot rely on anyone being what they seem.

This vigilance also seems to pull the trauma closer. When Martin lies awake at night scanning for danger, the memory returns not as a narrative but as isolated images, or else as raw emotional force without a picture. Watching others so closely during the day leaves him primed for the same flashes: a bicycle wheel, a woman’s sleeve, the crush of bodies in a crowded train. And because he keeps cutting off anger and clamping down on feeling, he never gets beyond those frozen moments. He cannot assemble a coherent story even for himself. The event remains a set of alarming fragments, which only strengthens his sense that the world no longer follows understandable rules.

Over time his habits have narrowed his life. He structures his practice to reduce situations in which he might be alone with women, lingers with his office door open between sessions, and avoids busy professional meetings when he can. Avoiding certain clothes, certain routes, certain kinds of contact has made the triggers more potent rather than less; bicycles stand out immediately, crowded rooms feel more charged, and female presence is noticed before anything else. His wife has seen how little sleep he gets and how much effort it takes for him to get through a workday that once felt natural. What finally brought him to seek help was the realization that he was beginning to organize even his clinical work around fear. He says he wants, at minimum, to be able to sit with a patient or walk past a bicycle rack without feeling that his whole body has to brace for harm, but what frightens him most is the possibility that this is what his life has become: permanently watchful, emotionally constricted, and unable to trust either other people or his own mind.
